Two Quiet Conditions

Lesson 1 at a glance

After the pictures

Our Group Agreement. Ask: “What do we need from each other so that everyone feels free to speak?” Make sure the group agrees on these points:

  • What we hear in the group stays in the group.
  • We do not laugh at or blame anyone for their condition, their weight or their numbers.
  • Each person comes with someone from the household whenever possible.
  • The volunteer is not a nurse. She does not change anyone’s medicine. For that, we go to the health worker.

Then agree on the day, time and place for meetings, and choose an Activity Leader.

Discuss barriers. Ask: “Is there anything that might prevent you from coming to these lessons with someone from your household?”

Request commitments. Ask: “Based on what you have heard today, what commitment will you make?” Each person chooses. Do not press anyone who is not ready.

Picture 1.1Story: Auntie Naa’s News

Picture 1.1 · text sideStory: Auntie Naa’s News

Read the story aloud.

Auntie Naa sells waakye at the lorry station. One morning, health workers come to the station to check blood pressure for free. The nurse tells Naa, “Your blood pressure is high. Please come to the mission hospital this week.”

Naa is afraid. She feels strong. How can she be sick? Her friend at the next table says, “BP? Someone has done this to you. It is spiritual.”

At home, Naa tells her husband, Uncle Kofi. He has had diabetes for three years. He often forgets his medicine. He laughs and says, “Me, I feel fine. Don’t worry yourself.”

That night Naa cannot sleep. She thinks of their neighbour, Mr. Mensah. He had a stroke last year. Now he cannot drive his taxi. Naa asks herself, “What should I do?”

Ask the group.

  • Why is Auntie Naa afraid?
  • What do people in our community say causes BP and sugar disease?
  • Uncle Kofi feels fine, so he does not worry. Do you know people like him?

Encourage discussion. Do not correct “wrong” answers. Let everyone give an opinion. This page is for discussion, not for teaching.

Say “Let us compare your ideas with the messages on the following pages.”

Picture 1.2Common Conditions, Not a Curse

Picture 1.2 · text sideCommon Conditions, Not a Curse

Ask: “What do you think these pictures mean?” Affirm the answers. Then share each message.

A

High blood pressure and diabetes are very common.

  • Out of every five adults in Ghana, about one has high blood pressure.
  • Out of every twenty adults, about one has diabetes.
  • Anyone can have them: men and women, rich and poor, fat and slim.
B

They are conditions of the body. They are not a curse.

  • They are not caused by witchcraft or by something a person did wrong.
  • A health worker can measure them with a simple test.
C

You cannot catch them from another person.

  • They do not pass by touching, eating together or sharing a room.
  • They can run in families. If you have one of them, your brothers, sisters and grown children should be checked too.

Ask the group.

  • Who in your family has BP or sugar disease?
  • How do people in our community treat someone who has one of these conditions?
Additional information for the facilitator

How common. The 2023 Ghana STEPS survey found that 21.7% of adults aged 18 to 69 had high blood pressure and 5.2% had raised fasting blood sugar. Other sources give higher figures for high blood pressure. Use “about one in five” with participants.

Words to use. Use the names people in the group already use for the two conditions. “Condition” is enough if “disease” makes people feel ashamed.

Beliefs. Do not argue about faith. Say that the conditions can be measured in the body and treated, and that a person can pray and take care of the body at the same time.

Picture 1.3Quiet Conditions That Can Harm

Picture 1.3 · text sideQuiet Conditions That Can Harm

Ask: “What do you think these pictures mean?” Affirm the answers. Then share each message.

A

You can feel well and still have high blood pressure or diabetes.

  • Most people with high blood pressure feel nothing.
  • Diabetes can stay hidden for years.
  • Many people in Ghana who have high blood pressure do not know it.
B

Without care, these conditions slowly harm the body.

  • They can cause a stroke.
  • They can harm the heart and the kidneys.
  • They can harm the eyes and cause blindness.
  • Diabetes can cause sores on the feet that do not heal.
C

The only way to know is to be checked.

  • A health worker checks blood pressure on the arm.
  • A health worker checks sugar with a small drop of blood.

There is good news. These conditions can be controlled. We will learn how at our next meeting.

Ask the group.

  • Uncle Kofi says, “I feel fine.” Is he right not to worry? Why?
  • When did you last have your blood pressure checked?
Additional information for the facilitator

No signs. The only way to detect high blood pressure is to have it measured. Headache, dizziness or “feeling the BP rise” are not reliable signs. In type 2 diabetes, signs can be mild or absent for several years.

Do not frighten. This page explains why a person who feels well still needs care. End on the good news: the conditions can be controlled, and Lesson 2 shows how.
